strategies.name: Current: Corn → Soybean
strategies.why: This is what the field has grown every year 2020–2025 (USDA CropScape). It is shown as the baseline to compare against.
evidence: Field cover from space (NASA MODIS NDVI): the field was bare ~0.7 months/yr in 2005–07 (pasture) but ~6.4 months/yr since 2015 under corn–soybean; winter greenness trend -0.048 NDVI/decade (Theil–Sen; Mann–Kendall p < 0.001, statistically significant). This rotation would leave it bare ~7.0 months/yr (current: 7.0).

Water: May–Sep crop water demand (ET0, NASA POWER) 769 mm vs rain (NASA GPM IMERG) 562 mm → shortfall 207 mm. NASA ECOSTRESS shows crops used only 50% of demand in Jul–Aug (water-limited). NASA daily water balance: this rotation's cash crops lack 17% of their water demand (current: 17%); modelled crop-water demand 611 mm/yr (current: 611 mm).
Soil moisture (NASA SMAP): 0.26 m³/m³ in Apr–May falling to 0.20 m³/m³ in Jul–Aug, when corn silks and soybeans fill pods.

Climate regimes (K-means on 21 growing seasons): 12 of 21 were 'Hot & dry', including 5 of the last 5 (2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025). Temperature trend +0.86 °C/decade (Theil–Sen; Mann–Kendall p = 0.09, not statistically significant).
FAO GAEZ climate suitability of the main crops: 3919/10000 (current: 3919).
Soil (USDA SSURGO): 3.0% organic matter, subsoil up to 45% clay, pH 6.1, erodibility Kw 0.33.

Yield history (USDA NASS, observed): in 2012 county yields fell 34% (corn), 27% (soybean), 30% (sorghum) below trend; winter wheat averaged 108% of trend in the hottest years. Secondary Random Forest check (held-out error ±11 points): with 2012 held out it predicted only 16% / 18% / 16% — it under-estimates extreme losses. Sources of the crop-loss values for this rotation's crops: Random Forest trained on all years (in-sample estimate, not validated).
information_gaps: Market potential is not income: crop prices, input costs and contracts are not modelled; the score reflects which crops are traded in Riley County (USDA NASS).
The water balance is an exploratory calibrated model: runoff and irrigation are not modelled and the claypan rooting limit is inferred from SSURGO.
County yields include irrigated fields, so the yield model cannot fairly rank corn vs. sorghum heat tolerance.
SMAP soil moisture is a 9 km average that mixes this field with its neighbours; ECOSTRESS observes on irregular days.
Crop-trait values are regional figures from K-State, UNL, USDA and peer-reviewed sources, not trials on this field.
risks_for_local_review: Corn: Highest water and nitrogen demand; yield most sensitive to water stress from tasseling through silking (mid–late July)
Soybean: Low residue after harvest leaves soil exposed; sensitive to drought during pod set and early bean fill (August)

strategies.why: Adds Cereal rye cover crop, Winter wheat, Hairy vetch cover crop to address the farm's main problems. Better than the current rotation on: erosion protection, pest break, water.
evidence: Field cover from space (NASA MODIS NDVI): the field was bare ~0.7 months/yr in 2005–07 (pasture) but ~6.4 months/yr since 2015 under corn–soybean; winter greenness trend -0.048 NDVI/decade (Theil–Sen; Mann–Kendall p < 0.001, statistically significant). This rotation would leave it bare ~1.0 months/yr (current: 7.0).

Water: May–Sep crop water demand (ET0, NASA POWER) 769 mm vs rain (NASA GPM IMERG) 562 mm → shortfall 207 mm. NASA ECOSTRESS shows crops used only 50% of demand in Jul–Aug (water-limited). NASA daily water balance: this rotation's cash crops lack 14% of their water demand (current: 17%); modelled crop-water demand 624 mm/yr (current: 611 mm).
Soil moisture (NASA SMAP): 0.26 m³/m³ in Apr–May falling to 0.20 m³/m³ in Jul–Aug, when corn silks and soybeans fill pods.

Climate regimes (K-means on 21 growing seasons): 12 of 21 were 'Hot & dry', including 5 of the last 5 (2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025). Temperature trend +0.86 °C/decade (Theil–Sen; Mann–Kendall p = 0.09, not statistically significant).
FAO GAEZ climate suitability of the main crops: 4167/10000 (current: 3919).
Soil (USDA SSURGO): 3.0% organic matter, subsoil up to 45% clay, pH 6.1, erodibility Kw 0.33.

Yield history (USDA NASS, observed): in 2012 county yields fell 34% (corn), 27% (soybean), 30% (sorghum) below trend; winter wheat averaged 108% of trend in the hottest years. Secondary Random Forest check (held-out error ±11 points): with 2012 held out it predicted only 16% / 18% / 16% — it under-estimates extreme losses. Sources of the crop-loss values for this rotation's crops: Calculated from USDA NASS county yields (observed, not a prediction); Random Forest trained on all years (in-sample estimate, not validated).
benefits: Cuts bare-soil time by 6.0 months/yr, protecting the soil from ~271 mm of off-season rain.
More roots and residue → builds organic matter and improves infiltration into the dense clay subsoil.
A legume in the rotation fixes nitrogen → lower fertilizer need for the following grass crop.
Less crop water stress in the NASA daily water balance: 14% of cash-crop water demand unmet vs 17% for the current rotation (2006–2025).
Lower drought-year risk: modelled relative yield in the driest quarter of seasons 78% vs 74% (FAO-33 Ky; modelled estimate, not a forecast).
More crop families → breaks corn rootworm and soybean pest cycles.
information_gaps: Market potential is not income: crop prices, input costs and contracts are not modelled; the score reflects which crops are traded in Riley County (USDA NASS).
The water balance is an exploratory calibrated model: runoff and irrigation are not modelled and the claypan rooting limit is inferred from SSURGO.
County yields include irrigated fields, so the yield model cannot fairly rank corn vs. sorghum heat tolerance.
SMAP soil moisture is a 9 km average that mixes this field with its neighbours; ECOSTRESS observes on irregular days.
Crop-trait values are regional figures from K-State, UNL, USDA and peer-reviewed sources, not trials on this field.
risks_for_local_review: Scores lower than the current rotation on: market potential.

Cereal rye cover crop: Before corn: terminate early (rye under ~8 in, ≥2 weeks before planting) to limit nitrogen tie-up — K-State recommends rye mainly before soybean; in a dry spring it uses moisture the next crop needs; seed and seeding cost; host of wheat streak mosaic virus and wheat curl mite (risk near wheat); after sorghum, establishment can be poor
Winter wheat: Needs a fall planting window after the summer crop; Hessian fly and rust risk; vulnerable to late spring freeze (e.g. April 2007)
Hairy vetch cover crop: Releases >70% of its nitrogen within two weeks of termination, so time termination close to planting; seed cost; can become a weed in wheat

known_limitations: EXPLORATORY CALIBRATED MODEL: water and drought-risk scores come from a daily soil-water balance (NASA GPM IMERG rain, NASA POWER ET0, SSURGO soil water above an inferred claypan rooting limit, FAO-56 stress, FAO-33 yield response).
